Structural body size over time in Atlantic Forest passerines

  • Show All Code
  • Hide All Code
  • View Source

A descriptive inquiry into four size proxies — wing, tail, tarsus, body mass

Author

Atlantic Birds project

Published

June 14, 2026

1 The puzzle, widened

The main analysis of this project found that wing length declined across 89 Atlantic Forest passerine species between 1990 and 2018 (Bayesian phylogenetic multilevel model, standardized year effect β = −0.73 mm per SD-year, 95 % CI −1.09 to −0.37, excluding zero), while a parallel model for log body mass found essentially no trend (β = −0.001 log-g per SD-year, 95 % CI −0.008 to +0.006). If birds are getting structurally smaller, why does their mass not shrink too?

This report explores that question descriptively across four proxies of body size: two flight-feather traits — wing length and tail length — a leg/skeletal trait, tarsus length, and the soft-tissue measure, body mass. Tarsus is conceptually the cleanest index of structural size; mass the crudest (it fluctuates with gut content, fat, hydration); the feather traits sit in between and additionally carry molt/wear signals. Throughout, we also track whether each bird was measured live or as a museum specimen, since preservation can bias measurements and could confound a temporal trend (developed in the descriptive section below and tested formally in Section 13). The result is richer than the original two-trait puzzle:

The four proxies do not move together. Within species, wing length declines, tarsus length increases, and tail length and body mass show no net change — so the wing decline is not a coordinated whole-body shrinkage. But the shape of the trends matters: wing length and tail length (the two feather traits) both fall sharply in the most recently sampled years, a recent signal a single linear slope hides.

2 Reproducing the analytical sample

We rebuild the exact analytical frame used by the project’s models directly from the raw ATLANTIC BIRD TRAITS csv (filters: Year ≥ 1990, adult, known sex, Passeriformes, inside the 20-km Atlantic Forest buffer; then species with ≥ 30 records and a ≥ 5-year span). This reproduces the canonical sample of 15,332 records / 89 species exactly. Wing, tail and tarsus each coalesce right/left/unspecified measurements the way the project’s wing variable is built.

Code 
RAW = "../data/raw/ATLANTIC_BIRD_TRAITS_completed_2018_11_d05.csv"
b = pd.read_csv(RAW, low_memory=False)

mask = (
    (b.Year >= 1990) & (b.Age == "Adult") &
    (b.Sex.isin(["Male", "Female"])) &          # R's filter drops NA sex too
    (b.Order == "Passeriformes") &
    (b.AtlanticForests_20km_Buffer == "inside the 20 km polygon")
)
d = b[mask].copy()
d["cwl"]  = (d["Wing_length_right.mm."].combine_first(d["Wing_length_left.mm."])
             .combine_first(d["Wing_length.mm."]))
d["ctail"] = (d["Tail_length_right.mm."].combine_first(d["Tail_length_left.mm."])
              .combine_first(d["Tail_length.mm."]))
d["ctar"] = (d["Tarsus_length_right.mm."].combine_first(d["Tarsus_length_left.mm."])
             .combine_first(d["Tarsus_length.mm."]))
d["Binomial"] = d["Binomial"].str.replace(" ", "_")
d = d[d.groupby("Binomial")["Binomial"].transform("size") >= 30].copy()
d = d[d.groupby("Binomial")["Year"].transform(lambda x: x.max() - x.min()) >= 5].copy()

d["scaled_yr"]  = (d.Year - d.Year.mean()) / d.Year.std()
d["scaled_lat"] = ((-d.Latitude_decimal_degrees) - (-d.Latitude_decimal_degrees).mean()) \
                   / (-d.Latitude_decimal_degrees).std()
d["mass"] = d["Body_mass.g."]
for resp, src in SRC.items():
    d[resp] = np.log(d[src])
YR_SD = d.Year.std()

print(f"Records: {len(d):,}   Species: {d.Binomial.nunique()}   (expect 15,332 / 89)\n")
print("Trait coverage within the sample (and species with ≥30 records of the trait):")
for resp in ORDER:
    src = SRC[resp]; sub = d.dropna(subset=[src])
    n30 = (sub.groupby("Binomial").size() >= 30).sum()
    print(f"  {LAB[resp]:14s}: {sub[src].notna().sum():>6,} records, "
          f"{sub.Binomial.nunique():>2} species ({n30} with ≥30)")
print(f"\nYear SD (for per-SD ↔ per-year conversion): {YR_SD:.2f} years")
Records: 15,332   Species: 89   (expect 15,332 / 89)

Trait coverage within the sample (and species with ≥30 records of the trait):
  wing length   :  9,864 records, 86 species (71 with ≥30)
  tail length   : 10,308 records, 86 species (69 with ≥30)
  tarsus length :  9,825 records, 86 species (69 with ≥30)
  body mass     : 13,761 records, 89 species (87 with ≥30)

Year SD (for per-SD ↔ per-year conversion): 5.37 years

All four traits are well sampled (~10,000–14,000 records). Body mass is actually the best sampled, so nothing here is limited by data volume.

3 A first note on data quality (tarsus)

Tarsus length contains some physically impossible values — passerine tarsi run roughly 10–35 mm, yet a handful exceed 50 mm (e.g. a 192 mm tarsus on a Herpsilochmus antwren, ~18 mm in life). These are data-entry errors. We keep all records in the main analysis for consistency with the project’s pipeline (which likewise keeps a 480 g mass outlier), but flag the issue here and show the tarsus trend is robust to removing implausible values — it even strengthens. A systematic, four-trait outlier analysis follows in Section 12.

Code 
def mixed_yr(df, resp):
    sub = df.dropna(subset=[resp]).copy()
    f = smf.mixedlm(f"{resp} ~ C(Sex) + scaled_yr + scaled_lat", sub,
                    groups=sub["Binomial"], re_formula="~scaled_yr").fit(method="lbfgs")
    b1, se = f.params["scaled_yr"], f.bse["scaled_yr"]
    return b1, se, f.pvalues["scaled_yr"], len(sub)

imp = d.ctar.notna() & ((d.ctar < 5) | (d.ctar > 40))
print(f"Implausible tarsus records (<5 or >40 mm): {imp.sum()} of {d.ctar.notna().sum()}")
for name, df in [("all records", d), ("plausible 5–40 mm only", d[~imp])]:
    b1, se, p, n = mixed_yr(df, "lntar")
    print(f"tarsus, {name:24s}: β_yr = {b1:+.4f} "
          f"[{b1-1.96*se:+.4f}, {b1+1.96*se:+.4f}], p = {p:.3f}, N = {n:,}")
Implausible tarsus records (<5 or >40 mm): 35 of 9825
tarsus, all records             : β_yr = +0.0117 [+0.0011, +0.0223], p = 0.030, N = 9,825
tarsus, plausible 5–40 mm only  : β_yr = +0.0129 [+0.0056, +0.0202], p = 0.001, N = 9,790

At the whole-sample scale the live and museum curves sit almost on top of each other, because between-species variation is enormous (and exactly why pooling across species, next, is the wrong tool). But that overlap hides the status effect: a 5 % shift in tail is invisible against a trait that varies several-fold across species. To expose it we re-plot the same data as within-species deviations (each record minus its species mean), which removes the between-species spread:

Code 
fig, ax = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(11, 6.5))
for a, resp in zip(ax.ravel(), ORDER):
    sub = ds.dropna(subset=[resp]).copy()
    sub["dev"] = (sub[resp] - sub.groupby("Binomial")[resp].transform("mean")) * 100
    for st, c in [("live", LIVE_C), ("museum", MUS_C)]:
        x = np.clip(sub.loc[sub.Status == st, "dev"], -25, 25)
        a.hist(x, bins=45, density=True, color=c, alpha=.5, label=st)
        a.axvline(sub.loc[sub.Status == st, "dev"].mean(), color=c, ls="--", lw=2)
    a.set_title(f"log {LAB[resp]}"); a.set_xlabel("within-species deviation (%)")
    a.set_ylabel("density"); a.legend()
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
Code 
rows = []
for resp in ORDER:
    src = SRC[resp]
    for st in ["live", "museum"]:
        x = ds.loc[(ds.Status == st), src].dropna()
        dev = (ds.loc[ds.Status == st, resp] -
               ds.groupby("Binomial")[resp].transform("mean")).dropna()
        rows.append([LAB[resp], st, f"{len(x):,}", f"{x.mean():.2f}", f"{x.median():.2f}",
                     f"{x.std()/x.mean():.3f}", f"{dev.mean()*100:+.2f}%"])
pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=["trait","status","n","mean","median","CV","mean within-spp dev"])

The descriptive table makes the point numerically: museum specimens read longer in tail (and slightly in tarsus) and lighter in mass, with wing barely touched. Since museum specimens are not evenly spread over time, we test whether this biases the trends in Section 13 — it does not for wing, tarsus or mass, and only matters for tail.

5 The trap: pooling across species reverses the sign

A naïve approach regresses each trait on year across all records at once, with the covariates the models use (sex, latitude).

Code 
rows = []
for resp in ORDER:
    sub = d.dropna(subset=[resp])
    f = smf.ols(f"{resp} ~ scaled_yr + C(Sex) + scaled_lat", data=sub).fit()
    b1 = f.params["scaled_yr"]; lo, hi = f.conf_int().loc["scaled_yr"]
    rows.append([f"log {LAB[resp]}", len(sub), fmt(b1), f"[{fmt(lo)}, {fmt(hi)}]"])
pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=["trait", "N", "β (per SD-yr, log)", "95% CI"])
trait N β (per SD-yr, log) 95% CI
0 log wing length 9864 +0.0093 [+0.0050, +0.0136]
1 log tail length 10308 +0.0164 [+0.0091, +0.0236]
2 log tarsus length 9825 +0.0200 [+0.0149, +0.0251]
3 log body mass 13761 +0.0203 [+0.0112, +0.0294]

Several naïve pooled slopes come out positive — including wing length, which we know declines within species. This is Simpson’s paradox: the pooled slope mixes genuine within-species change with shifts in which species were sampled over time, and between-species variation is so large that composition dominates. The pooled trend is uninformative. The right question is within-species, which the random-slope structure of the project’s models isolates — reproduced next.

6 Within-species trends: the four traits diverge

6.1 Per-species slopes

For each species we fit a within-species regression of the log trait on standardized year — the model-free analogue of a random year slope.

Code 
def per_species(resp):
    out = []
    for sp, g in d.dropna(subset=[resp]).groupby("Binomial"):
        if g.Year.nunique() < 3 or g[resp].nunique() < 2:
            continue
        out.append(smf.ols(f"{resp} ~ scaled_yr", data=g).fit().params["scaled_yr"])
    return np.array(out)

slopes = {r: per_species(r) for r in ORDER}
rows = []
for resp in ORDER:
    s = slopes[resp]; neg, pos = int((s < 0).sum()), int((s > 0).sum())
    sign_p = stats.binomtest(min(neg, pos), neg + pos).pvalue
    rows.append([f"log {LAB[resp]}", len(s), fmt(np.median(s)), fmt(s.mean()),
                 f"{pos}/{neg+pos}", f"{sign_p:.3f}"])
pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=["trait", "species", "median slope", "mean slope",
                            "increased", "sign-test p"])
trait species median slope mean slope increased sign-test p
0 log wing length 85 -0.0076 -0.0103 27/85 0.001
1 log tail length 85 -0.0043 +0.0015 38/85 0.386
2 log tarsus length 85 +0.0115 +0.0081 58/85 0.001
3 log body mass 89 -0.0073 -0.0029 38/89 0.203

bins = np.linspace(-0.06, 0.06, 31)
for a, resp in zip(ax.ravel(), ORDER):
    s = np.clip(slopes[resp], bins[0], bins[-1])
    a.hist(s, bins=bins, color=COL[resp], alpha=.8, edgecolor="white")

for a in ax[-1]: a.set_xlabel("within-species slope of log(trait) on standardized year")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

The four traits point different ways. Wing declines in most species (sign-test p = 0.001); tarsus increases in most (p = 0.001); tail and body mass are near coin-flips (p ≈ 0.4 and 0.2).

6.2 A like-for-like mixed model

Matching the project’s models without the phylogeny: a random-intercept / random-year-slope mixed model per trait (trait ~ sex + scaled_yr + scaled_lat + (1 + scaled_yr | species)).

Code 
rows = []
for resp in ORDER:
    b1, se, p, n = mixed_yr(d, resp)
    rows.append([f"log {LAB[resp]}", fmt(b1), f"[{fmt(b1-1.96*se)}, {fmt(b1+1.96*se)}]",
                 f"{p:.3f}", f"{n:,}"])
pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=["trait", "β year (per SD-yr, log)", "95% CI", "p", "N"])
trait β year (per SD-yr, log) 95% CI p N
0 log wing length -0.0105 [-0.0156, -0.0054] 0.000 9,864
1 log tail length +0.0025 [-0.0059, +0.0108] 0.560 10,308
2 log tarsus length +0.0117 [+0.0011, +0.0223] 0.030 9,825
3 log body mass -0.0023 [-0.0255, +0.0209] 0.845 13,761

Without any phylogenetic machinery this reproduces and extends the headline: wing length declines (CI excludes zero, p < 0.001), tarsus length increases (p ≈ 0.03; p = 0.001 once impossible values are dropped), and tail length and body mass show no net trend (CIs span zero). Three of the four proxies fail to show the wing decline; one moves the opposite way. The flat mass result is not a quirk of the Bayesian model, and the wing decline is clearly not a uniform skeletal shrinkage.

7 Putting all four traits on a common scale

The original “−0.73 vs −0.001” headline mixes units (mm vs log-grams). Expressing every within-species slope as a percentage change per decade (a log slope β ≈ a fractional change expm1(β)) makes them directly comparable.

Code 
res = {}
for resp in ORDER:
    b1, se, p, n = mixed_yr(d, resp); f = 10 / YR_SD
    res[resp] = (np.expm1(b1*f)*100, np.expm1((b1-1.96*se)*f)*100, np.expm1((b1+1.96*se)*f)*100)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.5, 3.3))
order = ["lnmass", "lntail", "lnwing", "lntar"]
for i, resp in enumerate(order):
    est, lo, hi = res[resp]
    ax.errorbar(est, i, xerr=[[est-lo],[hi-est]], fmt="o", color=COL[resp], ms=11, capsize=5, lw=2)
    ax.text(est, i+0.22, f"{est:+.2f}%/decade", ha="center", color=COL[resp], fontsize=10)
ax.axvline(0, color="black", lw=1)
ax.set_yticks(range(len(order))); ax.set_yticklabels([LAB[r] for r in order])
ax.set_ylim(-0.6, len(order)-0.3); ax.set_xlabel("within-species change per decade (%)")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
for resp in ORDER:
    e, l, h = res[resp]; print(f"  {LAB[resp]:14s}: {e:+.2f}%/dec  [{l:+.2f}, {h:+.2f}]")
  wing length   : -1.93%/dec  [-2.86, -0.99]
  tail length   : +0.46%/dec  [-1.08, +2.03]
  tarsus length : +2.20%/dec  [+0.21, +4.24]
  body mass     : -0.43%/dec  [-4.63, +3.96]

On a common footing, wing and tarsus change at similar magnitudes in opposite directions (~±2 %/decade), while tail length and body mass barely move. Body mass being flat is therefore corroborated by two other proxies, not explained away.

8 The shape of the trends over time (non-linearity within 1990–2018)

A single linear slope can hide acceleration, plateaus or reversals. We probe the shape of each trend two ways, both on within-species deviations (each record minus its species mean, so between-species composition is removed): (1) mean deviation in five time bins, and (2) a LOWESS smoother across years. We do not extend before 1990 — only ~1,250 records exist earlier, with essentially no body mass (one record before 1970) and likely different collection methods, so it would add high-leverage noise rather than signal.

Code 
BINS = [(1990,1999),(2000,2004),(2005,2009),(2010,2014),(2015,2018)]
centers = [np.mean(x) for x in BINS]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(12, 7.5), sharex=True)
for a, resp in zip(ax.ravel(), ORDER):
    sub = d.dropna(subset=[resp]).copy()
    sub["dev"] = (sub[resp] - sub.groupby("Binomial")[resp].transform("mean")) * 100
    lo = lowess(sub["dev"], sub["Year"], frac=0.6, return_sorted=True)
    a.plot(lo[:,0], lo[:,1], color=COL[resp], lw=2.5, zorder=3)
    for (lo_y, hi_y), c in zip(BINS, centers):
        v = sub[(sub.Year>=lo_y)&(sub.Year<=hi_y)]["dev"]
        a.errorbar(c, v.mean(), yerr=v.sem(), fmt="o", color=COL[resp], ms=7,
                   capsize=4, mec="white", zorder=4)
    a.axhline(0, color="black", lw=1)
    a.set_title(f"log {LAB[resp]}", loc="left"); a.set_ylabel("within-species deviation (%)")
for a in ax[-1]: a.set_xlabel("year")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
Code 
rows = []
for resp in ORDER:
    sub = d.dropna(subset=[resp]).copy()
    sub["dev"] = sub[resp] - sub.groupby("Binomial")[resp].transform("mean")
    sub["yr2"] = sub["scaled_yr"]**2
    f = smf.ols("dev ~ scaled_yr + yr2", data=sub).fit()
    rows.append([LAB[resp], fmt(f.params["scaled_yr"]), f"{f.pvalues['scaled_yr']:.3f}",
                 fmt(f.params["yr2"], 5), f"{f.pvalues['yr2']:.3f}"])
pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=["trait", "linear β", "linear p", "quadratic β", "quadratic p"])
trait linear β linear p quadratic β quadratic p
0 wing length -0.0111 0.000 -0.00489 0.000
1 tail length -0.0044 0.001 -0.00426 0.000
2 tarsus length +0.0109 0.000 +0.00078 0.487
3 body mass +0.0012 0.425 -0.00094 0.375

The temporal shape is itself informative:

  • Wing length declines non-linearly and recently: it sits slightly above the species mean through the 2000s and then drops sharply in 2015–2018 (~−1.7 %); the quadratic term is strongly negative (p < 0.001). The decline is concentrated in the most recent years rather than spread evenly across 28 years.
  • Tail length, though net flat, shows the same recent fall (~−1.7 % in 2015–2018; significant negative quadratic) — so the two feather traits move together in the recent window even though only wing has a significant linear trend. This hints at a shared recent flight-feather signal (true size change, or molt/wear/measurement shifts) that the linear model misses.
  • Tarsus length rises steadily and essentially linearly (quadratic n.s., p ≈ 0.49) — a monotone increase across the whole window.
  • Body mass stays on zero in every bin and shows no linear or quadratic term (both p > 0.3). There is no hidden non-linear mass change at any timescale.

8.1 Controlling for measurement status

Because the museum:live mix changes over time (Section 13), we re-draw each trajectory separately by status, centering within species and status so that each curve shows only the temporal shape within its own measurement type (the constant museum offset is removed).

Code 
fig, ax = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(12, 7.5), sharex=True)
for a, resp in zip(ax.ravel(), ORDER):
    sub = ds.dropna(subset=[resp]).copy()
    sub["dev"] = (sub[resp] - sub.groupby(["Binomial", "Status"])[resp].transform("mean")) * 100
    for st, c in [("live", LIVE_C), ("museum", MUS_C)]:
        g = sub[sub.Status == st]
        if len(g) > 30:
            lo = lowess(g["dev"], g["Year"], frac=0.6, return_sorted=True)
            a.plot(lo[:, 0], lo[:, 1], color=c, lw=2.5, label=st, zorder=3)
        for lo_y, hi_y in BINS:
            v = g[(g.Year >= lo_y) & (g.Year <= hi_y)]["dev"]
            if len(v) >= 15:
                a.errorbar(np.mean([lo_y, hi_y]), v.mean(), yerr=v.sem(), fmt="o",
                           color=c, ms=6, capsize=3, mec="white", zorder=4)
    a.axhline(0, color="black", lw=1)
    a.set_title(f"log {LAB[resp]}", loc="left")
    a.set_ylabel("within-(species×status) dev (%)"); a.legend(fontsize=9)
for a in ax[-1]: a.set_xlabel("year")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

7 body mass museum -0.60% (n263) -1.01% (n286) +0.60% (n440) +0.63% (n850) -2.40% (n146)

Read trait by trait, controlled by status:

  • Wing — the live series carries the whole story: gently above the species mean through the 2000s, then a sharp drop in 2015–2018 (−1.7 %). Museum wing is flat/noisy on a small sample and does not reproduce (or oppose) the decline.
  • Tarsus — the steady increase is clear in the live series (−1.6 % → +2.1 %); museum tarsus is erratic but ends positive too.
  • Tail — the hump-then-recent-fall holds in the live series; museum tail swings wildly (a function of ~200–440 records spread thinly across years) and is best disregarded for shape.
  • Body mass — flat in both status groups across every period; the only notable museum point is a 2015–2018 dip on just ~150 records, well within noise.

So the temporal shapes are properties of the live data, not of the changing museum fraction. Museum specimens are too few — and too unevenly spread across years — to define a trajectory, but where they appear they do not contradict the live series.

So “deeper time changes” exist — but as non-linearity within 1990–2018, not something recoverable by extending the record backward. The most striking is that the wing (and tail) decline is a recent phenomenon, robust to measurement status, which the project’s linear slope understates.

9 Signal-to-noise: how blunt is each instrument?

Part of why body mass is uninformative is that it is a much noisier index of size. We quantify this with the within-species coefficient of variation (CV) per trait (each on the species with ≥ 30 records of it).

Code 
cvrows = []
for resp in ORDER:
    src = SRC[resp]; sub = d.dropna(subset=[src])
    cvs = sub.groupby("Binomial").apply(lambda g: g[src].std()/g[src].mean()
                                        if len(g) >= 30 else np.nan).dropna()
    for v in cvs: cvrows.append((LAB[resp], v))
cv = pd.DataFrame(cvrows, columns=["trait", "cv"])

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.5, 4.3))
for j, resp in enumerate(ORDER):
    vals = cv.loc[cv.trait == LAB[resp], "cv"].values
    jit = np.random.RandomState(j).normal(0, .05, len(vals))
    ax.scatter(np.full(len(vals), j)+jit, vals, color=COL[resp], alpha=.65, edgecolor="white")
    ax.scatter(j, np.median(vals), color="black", marker="_", s=700, lw=2.5, zorder=3)
ax.set_xticks(range(len(ORDER))); ax.set_xticklabels([LAB[r] for r in ORDER])
ax.set_ylabel("within-species CV"); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

print("Median within-species CV:")
for resp in ORDER:
    print(f"  {LAB[resp]:14s}: {cv.loc[cv.trait==LAB[resp],'cv'].median():.3f}")
Median within-species CV:
  wing length   : 0.059
  tail length   : 0.093
  tarsus length : 0.119
  body mass     : 0.137

Body mass carries ~2.4× the within-species noise of wing length; tail and tarsus are intermediate. Noise is part of why mass is uninformative — but not the whole story: tarsus is noisier than wing yet still resolves a clear opposite trend, proving the flat traits cannot be blamed on noise alone.

10 Does the mass–wing relationship shift? (allometry / condition)

If wing shrinks while mass holds, are birds heavier for their wing? We regress log mass on log wing within species and test whether the residual (“mass-for-wing” condition index) trends over time.

Code 
bw = d.dropna(subset=["lnmass", "lnwing"]).copy()
allo = smf.mixedlm("lnmass ~ lnwing", bw, groups=bw["Binomial"],
                   re_formula="~lnwing").fit(method="lbfgs")
bw["cond"] = bw["lnmass"] - (allo.params["Intercept"] + allo.params["lnwing"]*bw["lnwing"])
ct = smf.mixedlm("cond ~ scaled_yr", bw, groups=bw["Binomial"],
                 re_formula="~scaled_yr").fit(method="lbfgs")
b1, se = ct.params["scaled_yr"], ct.bse["scaled_yr"]
print(f"Within-species allometric slope (log mass ~ log wing): {allo.params['lnwing']:.2f}")
print(f"Mass-for-wing (condition) trend: {b1:+.4f} [{b1-1.96*se:+.4f}, {b1+1.96*se:+.4f}] "
      f"per SD-yr, p = {ct.pvalues['scaled_yr']:.3f}")
Within-species allometric slope (log mass ~ log wing): 0.39
Mass-for-wing (condition) trend: +0.0047 [-0.0026, +0.0120] per SD-yr, p = 0.205

The within-species allometric slope is shallow (~0.4): wing explains only a modest fraction of individual mass variation, so the two are partly decoupled. The mass-for-wing residual shows no significant temporal trend (p ≈ 0.20). The size proxies are loosely yoked — a change in one need not appear in the others.

11 Sanity check: early-vs-late quartile comparison

The model-free comparison the project reports for each trait — mean log trait in the early (≤ 2006) vs late (≥ 2013) period, per species.

Code

def quartile(resp):
    t = (pq.dropna(subset=[resp]).groupby(["Binomial","period"])[resp].mean().unstack().dropna())
    return (t["late"] - t["early"]).sort_values()

for a, resp in zip(ax, ORDER):

    a.axhline(0, color="black", lw=1); a.set_xticks([])

The quartile picture matches the slopes: wing down, tarsus up, tail and mass split.

12 Within-species outliers and their influence on the trends

How far do the results depend on a few aberrant records within species? We detect within-species outliers with a robust rule, cross-check them against an independent signal (left vs right measurements), and re-estimate every trend with the outliers removed or tamed.

12.1 Detecting within-species outliers (robust MAD rule)

For each species and trait we compute a robust z-score on the log scale, z = (log x − median) / (1.4826 · MAD). Median/MAD are themselves resistant to outliers, so a single aberrant value cannot define the threshold. We flag |z| > 3.5.

Code 
def mad_z(df, resp):
    g = df.groupby("Binomial")[resp]
    med = g.transform("median")
    mad = g.transform(lambda x: (x - x.median()).abs().median()) * 1.4826
    return (df[resp] - med) / mad.replace(0, np.nan)

rows = []
for resp in ORDER:
    z = mad_z(d, resp); n = d[resp].notna().sum()
    rows.append([LAB[resp], f"{n:,}"] +
                [f"{(z.abs()>t).sum()} ({(z.abs()>t).mean()*100:.2f}%)" for t in (3.5, 4, 5)])
pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=["trait", "N", "|z|>3.5", "|z|>4", "|z|>5"])
trait N |z|>3.5 |z|>4 |z|>5
0 wing length 9,864 263 (1.72%) 199 (1.30%) 127 (0.83%)
1 tail length 10,308 325 (2.12%) 253 (1.65%) 169 (1.10%)
2 tarsus length 9,825 529 (3.45%) 370 (2.41%) 181 (1.18%)
3 body mass 13,761 440 (2.87%) 337 (2.20%) 214 (1.40%)

Outliers are uncommon in every trait (most frequent in tarsus, ~3.4 %; least in wing, ~1.7 %). The most extreme records are unambiguous data errors — decimal shifts, dropped digits, unit confusion:

Code 
worst = []
for resp in ORDER:
    src = SRC[resp]; z = mad_z(d, resp)
    tmp = d.assign(absz=z.abs()).nlargest(3, "absz")
    for _, r in tmp.iterrows():
        med = d.loc[d.Binomial == r.Binomial, src].median()
        worst.append([LAB[resp], r.Binomial.replace("_"," "), f"{r[src]:.1f}",
                      f"{med:.1f}", f"{r.absz:.0f}", int(r.Year)])

12.2 Cross-check: left vs right measurements

Where both sides were measured, the two should agree to within a couple of percent; large asymmetries flag error independently of the MAD rule. (Tail and mass have too few paired-side records to assess.)

Code

Tarsus is internally very consistent (median 1.1 %, one record above 10 %) — its errors are isolated gross values, not pervasive sloppiness. Wing, despite being least outlier-prone overall, carries more large left–right discrepancies: no trait is error-free.

12.3 Do the outliers change the trends?

We re-estimate each trait’s year trend under four treatments: all records, dropping |z|>4 and |z|>3.5, and winsorizing each species to its 1st–99th percentile. To avoid the random-slope mixed model’s numerical instability on trimmed subsets (its SEs inflate erratically when a few records are removed), we use a transparent, convergence-free estimator: the mean of within-species slopes, with a species-bootstrap 95 % CI.

Code 
def spp_slopes(df, resp):
    out = {}
    for sp, g in df.dropna(subset=[resp]).groupby("Binomial"):
        if g.Year.nunique() < 3 or g[resp].nunique() < 2: continue
        out[sp] = smf.ols(f"{resp} ~ scaled_yr", data=g).fit().params["scaled_yr"]
    return pd.Series(out)
def boot_ci(s, n=2000, seed=1):
    rng = np.random.RandomState(seed); v = s.values
    return np.percentile([rng.choice(v, len(v), replace=True).mean() for _ in range(n)], [2.5, 97.5])
def winsor(df, resp, lo=.01, hi=.99):
    df = df.copy()
    df[resp] = df.groupby("Binomial")[resp].transform(lambda x: x.clip(x.quantile(lo), x.quantile(hi)))
    return df

pd_ = lambda x: np.expm1(x * 10 / YR_SD) * 100
rules = ["all", "drop |z|>4", "drop |z|>3.5", "winsor 1–99%"]
sens = {}
for resp in ORDER:
    z = mad_z(d, resp)
    dsets = [d, d[~(z.abs()>4)], d[~(z.abs()>3.5)], winsor(d, resp)]
    sens[resp] = [tuple(pd_(np.r_[s.mean(), boot_ci(s)]))
                  for s in (spp_slopes(df, resp) for df in dsets)]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.5, 4.7))
off = {"lnwing": .24, "lntail": .08, "lntar": -.08, "lnmass": -.24}
for resp in ORDER:
    for i, (est, lo, hi) in enumerate(sens[resp]):
        ax.errorbar(est, i+off[resp], xerr=[[est-lo],[hi-est]], fmt="o", color=COL[resp],
                    ms=7, capsize=4, lw=1.7, label=LAB[resp] if i == 0 else None)
ax.axvline(0, color="black", lw=1)
ax.set_yticks(range(len(rules))); ax.set_yticklabels(rules)
ax.set_xlabel("year trend (% per decade, 95% bootstrap CI)")
ax.legend(loc="lower right", fontsize=9); ax.set_ylim(-0.6, len(rules)-0.4)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

print("Year trend (%/decade, species-bootstrap CI) by trait × rule:")
for resp in ORDER:
    print(f"  {LAB[resp]}:")
    for rule, (e, l, h) in zip(rules, sens[resp]):
        print(f"     {rule:14s}: {e:+.2f}% [{l:+.2f}, {h:+.2f}]")

The verdict is clean and trait-specific:

  • Body mass and tail length sit on/near zero under every treatment — no trend created or concealed by outliers.
  • Tarsus length stays positive and strengthens as errors are removed (~+2.2 % → ~+2.9 %/decade) — the opposite of outlier-driven.
  • Wing length stays negative with CI excluding zero under all four rules, attenuating modestly (~−1.9 % → ~−1.1 %/decade). Some magnitude rode on extreme records; direction and significance do not. (The mixed model loses significance for wing at one trimming threshold, but that is its SE inflating on the trimmed subset, not a reversal — the bootstrap above keeps wing firmly negative, which is why we prefer it here.)

Intra-species outliers do not drive any conclusion. If anything, cleaning the data sharpens the picture: tarsus up, wing down, tail and mass flat.

13 Does museum vs live measurement confound the trends?

The dataset’s Status field records whether each bird was measured live (mist-netting; 13,102 records here) or as a museum specimen (skin; 2,202 records). Museum skins can differ systematically from live birds — soft tissue desiccates, feathers can shrink or shift — so if the museum:live mix changed over time, a measurement artifact could masquerade as a temporal trend. We test this directly.

13.1 Museum specimens are concentrated in the early years

Code 
ds = d[d.Status.isin(["live", "museum"])].copy()
PER = [(1990,1999),(2000,2004),(2005,2009),(2010,2014),(2015,2018)]
print("Museum fraction of records by period:")
for lo, hi in PER:
    s = ds[(ds.Year >= lo) & (ds.Year <= hi)]
    print(f"  {lo}–{hi}: {100*(s.Status=='museum').mean():5.1f}% museum   (n = {len(s):,})")
print(f"\n  corr(museum indicator, year) = {np.corrcoef((ds.Status=='museum').astype(int), ds.Year)[0,1]:+.3f}")

This is exactly the setup for a confound: the museum share falls from ~41 % in the 1990s to ~6 % in 2015–2018. If museum specimens measure differently, that composition shift alone could induce an apparent trend.

13.2 Status shifts the measurements — strongly for tail and mass

We estimate the within-species museum-vs-live difference for each trait (trait ~ status + sex + latitude, species random intercept).

Code 
rows = []
for resp in ORDER:
    sub = ds.dropna(subset=[resp]).copy()
    f = smf.mixedlm(f"{resp} ~ C(Status) + C(Sex) + scaled_lat", sub,
                    groups=sub["Binomial"]).fit(method="lbfgs")
    c = f.params["C(Status)[T.museum]"]; se = f.bse["C(Status)[T.museum]"]
    rows.append([LAB[resp], f"{np.expm1(c)*100:+.2f}%",
                 f"[{np.expm1(c-1.96*se)*100:+.2f}, {np.expm1(c+1.96*se)*100:+.2f}]",
                 f"{f.pvalues['C(Status)[T.museum]']:.3f}", int((sub.Status=='museum').sum())])
pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=["trait", "museum vs live", "95% CI", "p", "n museum"])

Status genuinely affects the measurements: museum tail length reads ~5 % longer and museum body mass ~1.8 % lighter (both p < 0.001), museum tarsus ~1 % longer (p = 0.02), while wing length is essentially unaffected (+0.35 %, n.s.). Because museum specimens dominate the early years, these biases could in principle distort the temporal trends — so we re-estimate every trend four ways.

13.3 The trends are robust to status — with one caveat (tail)

Code 
def yreff(df, resp, extra=""):
    sub = df.dropna(subset=[resp]).copy()
    f = smf.mixedlm(f"{resp} ~ C(Sex)+scaled_yr+scaled_lat{extra}", sub,
                    groups=sub["Binomial"], re_formula="~scaled_yr").fit(method="lbfgs")
    b1, se = f.params["scaled_yr"], f.bse["scaled_yr"]; g = 10/YR_SD
    return (np.expm1(b1*g)*100, np.expm1((b1-1.96*se)*g)*100, np.expm1((b1+1.96*se)*g)*100,
            f.pvalues["scaled_yr"])

treat = ["all records", "+ Status covariate", "live-only", "museum-only"]
stat = {}
for resp in ORDER:
    stat[resp] = [yreff(ds, resp), yreff(ds, resp, "+C(Status)"),
                  yreff(ds[ds.Status=="live"], resp), yreff(ds[ds.Status=="museum"], resp)]

        ax.errorbar(est, i+off[resp], xerr=[[est-lo],[hi-est]], fmt="o", color=COL[resp],
                    ms=7, capsize=4, lw=1.7, label=LAB[resp] if i == 0 else None)
ax.axvline(0, color="black", lw=1)

ax.set_xlabel("year trend (% per decade, 95% CI)")

The picture is reassuring for three of four traits:

  • Wing length — decline robust everywhere: ~−1.9 %/decade at baseline, stronger once Status is controlled (−2.1 %) and on live-only records (−2.9 %, p < 0.001). Museum-only is the same direction (−1.1 %) but n.s. on its small, early sample. Since museum wing is barely different and museum records sit early, the confound if anything suppresses the decline slightly — the real signal is cleaner.
  • Tarsus length — increase robust and strengthens once status is controlled (+2.7 %) and on live-only (+3.2 %). Museum tarsus reads larger and sits early, so the confound partly masks the increase; removing it sharpens the signal.
  • Body mass — flat under every treatment (CI always spans zero). No status artifact creates or hides a mass trend.
  • Tail length — the caveat. Tail is the most status-sensitive trait (+5 % museum bias) and its weak signal flips with treatment: flat-to-negative on live-only (−0.4 %/decade) but strongly positive on the early, sparse museum records (+4.6 %). Any tail trend is therefore entangled with status and should be read from the live-only estimate.

Finally, the recent (2015–2018) feather-trait drop from Section 8 survives restricting to live birds — so it is not a museum artifact (the recent bins are ~94 % live anyway):

Code 
for resp, lab in [("lnwing","wing"), ("lntail","tail")]:
    for tag, sub0 in [("all ", ds), ("live", ds[ds.Status=="live"])]:
        sub = sub0.dropna(subset=[resp]).copy()
        sub["dev"] = (sub[resp] - sub.groupby("Binomial")[resp].transform("mean")) * 100
        v = sub[(sub.Year >= 2015) & (sub.Year <= 2018)]["dev"]
        print(f"  {lab} {tag}: 2015–2018 within-species deviation = {v.mean():+.2f}% (n {len(v)})")
  wing all : 2015–2018 within-species deviation = -1.68% (n 2064)
  wing live: 2015–2018 within-species deviation = -1.71% (n 2027)
  tail all : 2015–2018 within-species deviation = -1.74% (n 2014)
  tail live: 2015–2018 within-species deviation = -1.07% (n 1975)

Bottom line: museum-vs-live status is a real measurement effect and is confounded with time (museum early), but it does not drive the core inferences. Controlling for it leaves the wing decline and tarsus increase intact (both strengthen), and body mass flat. The only trait whose trend is genuinely status-dependent is tail length, whose net signal is weak and best taken from live-only records.

14 Conclusions

  1. The near-zero body-mass slope is real, not an artifact. It is reproduced by a plain within-species mixed model with no phylogeny (β ≈ −0.002 log/SD-yr, CI through zero), rests on more data than the wing analysis, and is precisely estimated rather than merely uncertain.

  2. Four size proxies, four behaviours — they do not move together. Within species: wing length declines (~−2 %/decade), tarsus length increases (~+2 %/decade), and tail length and body mass show no net change. Both directional results have sign-test p = 0.001, and tarsus strengthens when impossible values are removed.

  3. So this is not a uniform body-size reduction. A whole-body Bergmann-style shrinkage would pull tarsus, tail and mass down with wing; instead tarsus rises and tail and mass are flat. The net change is trait-specific to wing length, cautioning against reading the wing decline as general “shrinking body size.”

  4. But the temporal shape adds nuance (Section 8). The wing decline is non-linear and recent — concentrated in 2015–2018 (significant negative quadratic) — and tail length, the other feather trait, falls in the same recent window despite a flat net trend. At fine temporal resolution the two flight-feather traits align recently, which a single linear slope hides and which is worth following up (true recent size change vs molt/wear/measurement).

  5. “Deeper time” means non-linearity, not a longer record. Extending before 1990 is not advisable: only ~1,250 records exist earlier, with essentially no body mass (one record before 1970) and likely different methods. Sampling is itself back-loaded (the 1990s contribute < 1,000 records vs > 16,000 after 2000), so the trends are anchored by recent decades — all the more reason to read them through the non-linear lens above.

  6. Body mass being flat is corroborated, not just unresolved. Mass is the noisiest proxy (~2.4× the within-species CV of wing), lowering its power — but tarsus, though noisier than wing, resolves a clear opposite trend, so noise alone cannot explain the flat traits. Shallow mass–wing allometry (~0.4) and a non-trending condition index confirm the proxies are loosely coupled.

  7. The trends survive intra-species outlier handling (Section 12). Outliers are uncommon (1.7–3.4 %) and, where extreme, clearly clerical. Dropping or winsorizing them changes nothing essential: mass and tail stay flat, tarsus stays positive (strengthening), wing stays negative (attenuating).

  8. The trends survive the museum-vs-live confound (Section 13). Status is a real measurement effect (museum tail +5 %, mass −1.8 %, tarsus +1 %, wing negligible) and is confounded with time (museum specimens are concentrated in the early years), but it does not drive the inferences: controlling for status or restricting to live birds leaves the wing decline and tarsus increase intact (both strengthen) and mass flat. The recent feather-trait drop holds on live-only data. The one trait whose trend is genuinely status-dependent is tail length — weak and best read from live-only records.

  9. Methodological cautions. Naïve pooling across species reverses the sign of the trends (Simpson’s paradox). Tarsus carries the most measurement heterogeneity, so its direction is trustworthy but its magnitude approximate; tail/body-length-type feather and axial traits are noisier still. The random-slope mixed model can give unstable SEs on trimmed subsets, so robustness is best read from the species-bootstrap estimator. New trait results (tail, tarsus) and the recent-decline signal should be confirmed with the project’s phylogenetic model before being reported alongside wing.

In short: bringing in tail length and tarsus shows the wing-length decline is specific, not a coordinated body-size reduction — body mass does not decline because there is no whole-body shrinkage to detect. Yet the two feather traits fall together in the most recent years, a non-linear signal that deserves a closer look.
